/-!
# Erdős Problem 982

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/982](https://www.erdosproblems.com/982)
-/

@[expose] public section

open EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos982

/--
If $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ form a convex polygon then some vertex has at least
$\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor$ different distances to other vertices.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_982 (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) (p : Fin n → ℝ²) (hp : Function.Injective p)
    (hp' : EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon p) :
    ∃ (i : Fin n), { d : ℝ | ∃ j : Fin n, j ≠ i ∧ d = dist (p i) (p j) }.ncard ≥ n / 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos982

reformulations.difference: The source quantifies over unordered sets of n distinct points that 'form a convex polygon'. The Lean quantifies over indexed families `p : Fin n → ℝ²` with `3 ≤ n`, `Function.Injective p` and `EuclideanGeometry.IsConvexPolygon p`. That predicate says every triple i < j < k has oriented-angle sign 1, for p or for its reversal i ↦ p (-i). So the Lean additionally requires (a) the vertices to be listed in cyclic order and (b) strict convexity (no three collinear). It also restricts to n ≥ 3 and carries a redundant injectivity hypothesis.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (1) The conclusion `∃ i, #{dist (p i) (p j) : j ≠ i} ≥ n / 2` does not change when p is precomposed with a permutation σ of Fin n: the distance set of vertex i of p ∘ σ is the distance set of vertex σ i of p. (2) Any n ≥ 3 points in strictly convex position, listed in cyclic order along the hull (in the right direction, or reversed via i ↦ -i), have all triples i<j<k in the same orientation, so some listing satisfies `IsConvexPolygon`. (3) Conversely, if all triples i<j<k have the same nonzero orientation, then for every consecutive pair (i, i+1), and for (n-1, 0), all other points lie strictly on one side of that line. Hence every point is an extreme point: the image is strictly convex and p is injective. (4) Strict convexity is the source's meaning: Nivasch–Pach–Pinchasi–Zerbib, whose paper erdosproblems.com cites, define convex position as 'form the vertex set of a convex n-gon' and note 'every set in convex position is also in general position'. (5) `3 ≤ n` drops only n ≤ 2: n = 1 and n = 2 are trivially true, and n = 0 has no vertex, so a lower bound on n is needed. Lean checks I ran: `IsCcwConvexPolygon` forces injectivity for n ≥ 3; `IsConvexPolygon` holds for the unit square listed clockwise (left disjunct) and counter-clockwise (right disjunct via the reversal), and fails for the crossing 'bow-tie' order; the n = 3 case is provable in a few lines; for n = 0 the conclusion is false while `IsConvexPolygon` holds vacuously. I did not formalize the general equivalence, steps (2)–(3).
